clue.text: People left, returning by taxi: transport for the upwardly-mobile

parts.note: a cab is a taxi

indicators.note: returning means the phrase for people left is read backwards

parts.note: a race is a people, an ethnic group

explanation.surface: A crowd departs, coming home by taxi, and the clue tacks on a jibe about how social climbers travel.
explanation.walkthrough: 'returning' turns RACE + L into LECAR, which goes after CAB. 'upwardly-mobile' is meant literally: this transport climbs hills.
explanation.definitionFit: A cable car hauls passengers uphill on a wire, so it carries people who are literally moving upwards.

clue.text: Fruit dessert mostly put together in clumsy fashion

indicators.note: mostly means the word loses its final letter, leaving most of it

parts.note: a cobbler is a baked fruit pudding with a scone topping

explanation.surface: A fruit pudding that was mostly thrown together rather carelessly.
explanation.walkthrough: 'mostly' drops the last letter R from COBBLER.
explanation.definitionFit: To cobble something is to assemble it roughly or hastily, as in cobbling together a plan.

clue.text: Attack American women's team?

parts.note: broad is American slang for a woman, so broads' (here written BROADS) is American women's
a side is a team in sport

explanation.surface: Is this a question about an assault mounted by a women's team from the USA?
explanation.walkthrough: BROAD is US slang for a woman, so the women's team is the BROADS' SIDE.
explanation.definitionFit: A broadside is a forceful verbal or written assault, from the simultaneous firing of all guns on one side of a warship.

clue.text: Outstanding report written up on new pupil at public school

indicators.note: in a down clue, written up means these words are read from the bottom upwards, i.e. backwards

parts.note: A1 means first-rate, outstanding; the digit 1 serves as the letter I
a note is a short written report or memo

explanation.surface: A glowing school report has been written up on a fresh pupil at a public school.
explanation.walkthrough: 'written up' turns A1 + NOTE into ETONIA, and N goes after it. A1 means first-class; Eton is England's best-known public (fee-paying) school.
explanation.definitionFit: An Etonian is a pupil at Eton College, the famous English fee-paying boarding school.

clue.text: Scotsman's leader dismissed American sect

indicators.note: the leader of a word is its first letter, and dismissed means it is dropped

parts.note: Hamish is a typically Scottish first name, so stands for a Scotsman

explanation.surface: A Scotsman's boss has been sacked by an American religious group.
explanation.walkthrough: 'leader dismissed' drops the first letter H from HAMISH, a stock Scottish name.
explanation.definitionFit: The Amish are a traditionalist Anabaptist Christian community living mainly in Pennsylvania and Ohio.

clue.text: Wretched sailor caught boarding plane

parts.note: AB, able-bodied seaman, is a crossword sailor

indicators.note: boarding means getting on, so the letter for caught goes inside the plane

parts.note: a jet is an aeroplane
C is the cricket abbreviation for caught

explanation.surface: A miserable sailor is arrested just as he gets on a plane.
explanation.walkthrough: 'boarding' puts C inside JET, after AB.
explanation.definitionFit: Abject means miserable and hopeless, as in abject poverty.

clue.text: Second record pile of stuff still to be dealt with?

definitions.text: pile of stuff still to be dealt with?

parts.note: to second is to back or support someone
a log is a written record, as of a voyage

explanation.surface: Supporting a record seems to leave a heap of things still to deal with.
explanation.definitionFit: A backlog is an accumulation of unfinished work or orders still awaiting attention.

clue.text: East European turns to run off

indicators.note: turns means the phrase East European is read backwards as a whole

parts.note: a Pole is a European from Poland

explanation.surface: An eastern European decides to bolt.
explanation.walkthrough: 'turns' reverses E + POLE as one run, giving the answer.
explanation.definitionFit: To elope is to run away secretly, usually to marry.

clue.text: Observe what petty bank thief might do?

definitions.text: what petty bank thief might do?

explanation.surface: Is keeping watch what a small-time bank robber gets up to?
explanation.walkthrough: The second reading takes note literally: a petty thief at a bank pockets a single banknote.
explanation.definitionFit: To take note is to pay attention; literally a thief might also grab a banknote.

clue.text: Rescues characters from Las Vegas

indicators.note: the letters, or characters, of the words are taken and rearranged into a new word

explanation.surface: Someone saves people from the dangers of the Las Vegas strip.
explanation.walkthrough: 'characters from' tells you to rearrange the letters of LAS VEGAS.
explanation.definitionFit: To salvage is to save goods or people from wreckage or loss.

clue.text: The time of one's life?

parts.note: read literally, the timekeeper inside a living body, an innate rhythm that tracks one's age and cycles, not a wonderful experience

explanation.surface: A phrase for a wonderful experience, asked as a question.
explanation.walkthrough: The idiom 'the time of one's life' means a great experience; taken literally it is the body's internal timer.
explanation.definitionFit: This phrase names the innate mechanism regulating the body's cycles, especially the fertile years.

clue.text: Did lash out, just like a rowdy youngster

indicators.note: out signals these letters are shaken loose and rearranged

explanation.surface: Someone lashed out in temper, behaving like a yob.
explanation.walkthrough: 'out' asks you to rearrange the letters of DID LASH.
explanation.definitionFit: Laddish describes the boisterous, boozy behaviour of young men, a British term for rowdiness.

clue.text: Serf, indisposed, in a mood

indicators.note: in places the word for indisposed inside the word for mood

parts.note: a vein is a mood or manner, as in 'in a playful vein'
indisposed means ill

explanation.surface: A peasant is unwell and in a bad mood.
explanation.walkthrough: 'in' puts ILL inside VEIN.
explanation.definitionFit: A villein was a feudal peasant tied to a lord's land, a kind of serf.

clue.text: Lots of wine and a drop of spirits, say, somewhere in Canada

indicators.note: lots of means most of the word is kept, so its final letter goes

parts.note: a nip is a small measure of spirits
say means for example, abbreviated eg

explanation.surface: Plenty of wine and a little whisky, perhaps, at some Canadian location.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Lots of' cuts WINE to WIN.
explanation.definitionFit: Winnipeg is the capital city of the Canadian province of Manitoba.

clue.text: Train adverts

explanation.surface: Two words that seem to be about advertising on a train.
explanation.walkthrough: Puff-puff is a child's word for a steam train; puffs are also exaggerated plugs, so two of them are adverts.
explanation.definitionFit: Nursery speech names a steam locomotive after its chuffing; puff also means promotional blurb.

clue.text: Allowance made for former president

explanation.surface: An allowance has been made for an ex-president.
explanation.walkthrough: Ulysses S. Grant was the 18th President of the United States.
explanation.definitionFit: A grant is money awarded or allowed; Ulysses S. Grant led the USA after the Civil War.

clue.text: Bug installed by a dishonest dealer revealing evidence of wealth

indicators.note: installed by means the illness is placed inside the dealer's words

parts.note: a fence is someone who deals in stolen goods
a bug is an illness such as flu

explanation.surface: A listening bug planted by a crooked trader exposes signs of someone's riches.
explanation.walkthrough: 'installed by' puts FLU inside A FENCE, after its F. 'Bug' reads as a spy device but is an illness.
explanation.definitionFit: Affluence is wealth and abundance, and its visible signs show prosperity.

clue.text: Moorish soldiers entering place of worship

indicators.note: entering means the soldiers go inside the place of worship

parts.note: a mosque is a Muslim place of worship
RE, the Royal Engineers, are British Army soldiers

explanation.surface: Moorish troops are marching into a temple.
explanation.walkthrough: 'entering' puts RE (Royal Engineers) inside MOSQUE, after MO.
explanation.definitionFit: Moresque describes art or decoration in the Moorish style.

clue.text: Former Olympic athlete has energy in reserve

indicators.note: in reserve means the energy is held, kept within, the word for has

parts.note: to have something is to own it
E is the physics symbol for energy

explanation.surface: An old Olympian still has some energy left in the tank.
explanation.walkthrough: 'in reserve' keeps E inside OWNS. Jesse Owens won four golds at the 1936 Berlin Olympics.
explanation.definitionFit: Jesse Owens was the American sprinter and long jumper who starred at the 1936 Games.

clue.text: Indian dramatist born in France

parts.note: George Bernard Shaw was an Irish playwright
née is French for born, used before a maiden name

explanation.surface: An Indian playwright who was born in France.
explanation.definitionFit: The Shawnee are a Native American people, once of the Ohio valley, so Indian in the old sense.

clue.text: Scold Mrs Sprat?

explanation.surface: Is the wife of Jack Sprat, the nursery-rhyme man, a nag?
explanation.walkthrough: A sprat is a small fish, so Mrs Sprat is a fish's wife. In the nursery rhyme, Jack Sprat could eat no fat and his wife no lean.
explanation.definitionFit: A fishwife is a coarse-tongued, shrill woman, so a scold or nag.

clue.text: Oddball driver regularly goes under dam

indicators.note: in a down clue, goes under means the second piece sits beneath the first

parts.note: a weir is a low dam across a river

indicators.note: regularly means every other letter of driver is taken

explanation.surface: An eccentric motorist regularly passes below a dam.
explanation.walkthrough: 'regularly' takes D, I and E from DRIVER; 'goes under' sets them below WEIR.
explanation.definitionFit: A weirdie is an eccentric or strange person.

clue.text: Breed of cattle providing wool?

explanation.surface: A cattle breed that apparently produces wool.
explanation.walkthrough: A jersey is a knitted woollen jumper, a British word for a sweater.
explanation.definitionFit: Jersey cows are a dairy breed from the Channel Islands; a jersey is also a knitted sweater.

clue.text: Embrace unspecified number in foreign places

indicators.note: in places the number letter inside the rearranged places
foreign means strange or alien, so the letters of places are made unfamiliar

parts.note: N stands for an unspecified number in algebra

explanation.surface: Someone embraces any number of people in faraway lands.
explanation.walkthrough: 'foreign' rearranges PLACES to ECLASP and 'in' puts N inside it after E.
explanation.definitionFit: To enclasp is to hold someone in a clasp, an embrace.

clue.text: Conservative/Labour split

parts.note: Labour is the party of the left in British politics

explanation.surface: A split between the Conservative and Labour parties in Britain.
explanation.walkthrough: Labour is the main left-wing party in Britain, the Conservatives the right.
explanation.definitionFit: Cleft means split or divided, as in a cleft chin.

clue.text: Newspaper stand?

explanation.surface: A two-word query about a newspaper kiosk.
explanation.walkthrough: Tribune is a common newspaper title, such as the Chicago Tribune; a tribune is also a raised platform for a speaker.
explanation.definitionFit: Many papers are called the Tribune; a tribune is a dais or rostrum one stands on.

clue.text: Gangster, however, out of heroin

indicators.note: out of means the heroin letter is taken out of the word for however

parts.note: though means however, as in 'it rained, though'
H is slang for heroin

explanation.surface: A gangster has run out of heroin, though.
explanation.walkthrough: 'out of' removes the H from THOUGH.
explanation.definitionFit: A tough is a violent thug, the kind of hoodlum a gang employs.

clue.text: Victoria sponge an ingredient of this dessert?

definitions.text: Victoria sponge an ingredient of this dessert?

parts.words: Victoria sponge an ingredient of this dessert?
parts.note: Victoria is read as the monarch, so the pudding is named as a royal ruler among desserts, not a cake recipe

explanation.surface: Is a Victoria sponge cake part of this pudding?
explanation.walkthrough: Victoria sponge is a jam sandwich cake named after Queen Victoria; the clue reads her as a queen of puddings, a British baked custard with jam and meringue.
explanation.definitionFit: This traditional British pudding is breadcrumb custard topped with jam and meringue, named as regal among sweets.

clue.text: Book sought in earnest here

indicators.note: sought in means the answer is searched for within the following words

explanation.surface: A book is earnestly looked for here.
explanation.walkthrough: 'sought in' points to the run inside 'earnEST HERe'.
explanation.definitionFit: Esther is a book of the Old Testament telling of a Jewish queen of Persia.

clue.text: One's always taken in by your criminal activity

indicators.note: taken in by means the first words are placed inside the word for your

parts.note: thy is the old form of your
one is I, the Roman numeral; the 's is 'is', a link
ever means always

explanation.surface: Someone is permanently deceived by your crooked behaviour.
explanation.walkthrough: 'taken in by' puts I + EVER inside THY, after TH.
explanation.definitionFit: Thievery is the practice of stealing, an illegal pursuit.
